definition: Behavioral mimicry is an implicit social behavior in which a person mirrors another person’s behavior during interaction. In the source material, it is described as emerging in early childhood and as part of the developing set of social behaviors used to coordinate with others.

reasons: The packet does not support the specific characterization that behavioral mimicry is “mirroring another person’s behavior during interaction.” It only states that it is an “implicit behavior thought to develop during early childhood” and discusses interaction behaviors broadly (including imitation/coordination tasks) without defining behavioral mimicry as mirroring.

The packet mentions early childhood development, but it does not describe mimicry as “part of the developing set of social behaviors used to coordinate with others.” It notes that roles in early social interactions remain unknown and does not assert that mimicry coordinates with others.

The packet supports that behavioral mimicry is an implicit behavior thought to develop during early childhood, but it does not explicitly support the added gloss that it means mirroring another person's behavior during interaction.

The packet does not support the claim that behavioral mimicry is part of a developing set of social behaviors used to coordinate with others; it only says early development of implicit social behaviors remains uncertain and mentions coordination in a broader discussion of interaction behaviors.
